## TidyTuesday Part (Optional)

::: {.callout-important title="Instructions"}
You can count work on this week's TidyTuesday toward the exceptional work.
:::
```{r}
library(tidyverse)

majors <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-10-20/ai_salary_majors.csv")

glimpse(majors)
names(majors)
nrow(majors)
```

```{r}
majors |>
  summarise(number_of_majors = n(), missing_salary = sum(is.na(median_starting_salary)), missing_exposure = sum(is.na(ai_exposure_percentile)))
```
Background info: This dataset combines information on 285 U.S. college majors. For each major, it includes median earnings one year after bachelor degree completion and a measure of how much its related occupations overlap with AI capabilities. The AI exposure percentile runs from 0 to 100 among the majors. AI exposure is not the same as the probability of being replaced by AI: AI might also help workers with their tasks.

Research question:Do college majors with lower AI exposure have higher starting salaries, and how does this relationship vary across fields of study?

```{r}
major_clean <- majors |>
  filter(!is.na(field_of_study), !is.na(broad_field_short), !is.na(median_starting_salary), !is.na(ai_exposure_percentile))

major_clean |>
  summarise(number_of_majors = n(), median_salary = median(median_starting_salary), median_exposure_percentile = median(ai_exposure_percentile),
    salary_exposure_correlation = cor(median_starting_salary, ai_exposure_percentile))
```

```{r}
ggplot(major_clean, aes(x = ai_exposure_percentile, y = median_starting_salary)) + 
  geom_point(color = "#39758A", alpha = 0.65, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#C07855", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100), limits = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Median earnings one year after graduation across college majors",
    subtitle = "Higher AI exposure does not clearly predict lower starting pay",
    x = "AI exposure percentile (0 = least exposed; 100 = most exposed)", y = "Median starting salary (USD)",
    caption = "Graphic by Andy Zhu | Source: College Scorecard and AIOE, via TidyTuesday (2026-10-20).\nEach point represents one major. Exposure is not a measure of job replacement.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), 
        plot.caption.position = "plot", plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8))
```
The relationship between AI exposure and starting salary is weak in this dataset. Majors with similar AI exposure scores can have very different starting salaries, a lower AI exposure percentile does not necessarily imply higher starting pay.

```{r}
top_fields <- major_clean |>
  count(broad_field_short, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  pull(broad_field_short)

field_data <- major_clean |>
  filter(broad_field_short %in% top_fields)

field_data |>
  group_by(broad_field_short) |>
  summarise(number_of_majors = n(), median_ai_exposure = median(ai_exposure_percentile), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(median_ai_exposure)
```

```{r}
ggplot(field_data, aes(x = ai_exposure_percentile, y = fct_reorder(broad_field_short, ai_exposure_percentile, .fun = median))) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#A7C8D8", outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey45") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100), limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "AI exposure varies across and within fields of study",
    subtitle = "The eight broad fields containing the most majors in the dataset",
    x = "AI exposure percentile (0 = least exposed; 100 = most exposed)", y = NULL,
    caption = "Graphic by [Your Name] | Source: College Scorecard and AIOE, via TidyTuesday (2026-10-20).\nEach box summarizes majors, not individual graduates; dashed line marks the 50th percentile.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), plot.caption.position = "plot", plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8))
```
Broad fields differ in their typical AI exposure, but the boxes and whiskers also show variation among majors within the same field. Consequently, broad subject labels cannot fully describe a graduate's potential AI exposure.

```{r}
least_exposed <- major_clean |>
  arrange(ai_exposure_percentile) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  mutate(exposure_group = "Least exposed*")

most_exposed <- major_clean |>
  arrange(desc(ai_exposure_percentile)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  mutate(exposure_group = "Most exposed*")

extreme_majors <- bind_rows(least_exposed, most_exposed) |>
  mutate(major_label = case_when(
      field_of_study == "Building/Construction Finishing, Management, and Inspection" ~ "Construction",
      field_of_study == "Heavy/Industrial Equipment Maintenance Technologies/Technicians" ~ "Industrial Equipment",
      field_of_study == "English Language and Literature/Letters, Other" ~ "English Literature",
      field_of_study == "International/Globalization Studies" ~ "Global Studies",
      field_of_study == "Business/Managerial Economics" ~ "Business Economics",
      field_of_study == "Peace Studies and Conflict Resolution" ~ "Peace Studies",
      TRUE ~ field_of_study),
    exposure_group = factor(exposure_group, levels = c("Least exposed*", "Most exposed*")))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.8

ggplot(extreme_majors, aes(x = median_starting_salary, y = fct_reorder(major_label, median_starting_salary), fill = exposure_group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::dollar(median_starting_salary)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Least exposed*" = "darkblue", "Most exposed*" = "orange")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(title = "Starting salaries for the five least and five most AI-exposed majors",
    subtitle = "Low AI exposure does not guarantee high starting pay",
    x = "Median earnings one year after graduation (USD)", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
    caption = paste("Graphic by Andy Zhu | Source: College Scorecard and AIOE, via TidyTuesday (2026-10-20).",
      "\n* 'Least exposed' = the five majors with the lowest AI exposure percentile;",
      "'Most exposed' = the five majors with the highest AI exposure percentile.",
      "\nMajors were selected by AI exposure, not by earnings; some salary estimates rely on relatively few institutions.")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top", plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), plot.caption.position = "plot", 
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey40", margin = margin(t = 12), lineheight = 1.1))
```
The five least AI-exposed majors include both higher and lower paying programs. This comparison shows why ranking majors on AI exposure alone is not sufficient for evaluating their economic prospects. It also shows the range of salaries at both ends of the exposure distribution. Since a few majors draw on a small number of colleges, these examples should not be treated as predictions of an individual student's salary.

In Conclusion, the data show a weak relationship between AI exposure and starting salary across majors. Exposure differs across fields and majors within the same field, while the salaries of high or low exposed majors can vary a lot. Students considering a major may therefore want to evaluate both earnings and the kinds of skills they need. Also, AI exposure measures overlap with AI capabilities, it does not measure the probability that graduates will lose their jobs because of AI.
